earlier: I don't think the mind ever extends past the body. Tools are tools.
later: It isn't true that my mental states stop at my skin. My notebook is not just a tool, it's not separate from my memory at all.

earlier: Every single fact has an explanation, even if we'll never find it.
later: I think, probably, some facts are just brute. The universe existing at all might have no reason behind it whatsoever.

earlier: A statue and its clay are one object, there's no second thing sitting in the same place.
later: Probably the statue and the lump are two different objects. They have different persistence conditions, so I kind of have to say two.

earlier: I think philosophy has come a long way. We have much better arguments and distinctions now, and that adds up to a substantial amount of progress.
later: I am less confident about calling the progress huge after reading those old debates again. The smaller gains account has some appeal, but I have not settled on it.

earlier: I count a belief as justified partly by how reliably it was formed. Someone can have that going for them without being able to establish it just by looking inward.
later: I'm trying to summarize the author accurately: she says justification is settled entirely by what the believer can access through reflection. That's her position in the chapter, not a commitment I'm making here.

earlier: I don't think any fact is just there for absolutely no reason. We can fail to find an explanation, sure, but that doesn't mean there isn't one to find.
later: My position is still that nothing about reality is explanationless. Even if the answer is permanently beyond us, there's something that accounts for every fact being the way it is.

earlier: I think a life gets all its meaning from the commitments and interests of the person living it. Nothing becomes meaningful for me independently of what I care about or choose.
later: If caring for strangers gave a life meaning independently of anyone’s commitments, then even an unwilling helper could have a meaningful life through that work. I am exploring that premise, not saying I accept it.

earlier: I think arguments about what exists can be about serious features of reality. Getting our words straight isn't enough; the world itself settles whether the disputed things are actually there.
later: If existence questions really could be settled just by sorting out our concepts and language, I'd expect a lot of these debates to end pretty quickly. That's a hypothetical consequence, not a claim that the premise is true.

earlier: I think reason can get us to some real truths about the world without borrowing them from sensory evidence. Observation is useful, but it is not the only possible foundation.
later: I do not think a good reason for an action has to come from an existing desire. Sometimes I have reason to keep a promise despite wanting nothing it will bring me.

earlier: I think genes are the fundamental things natural selection sorts. Bodies come and go, but the copying and persistence of genetic variants is the basic process I am tracking.
later: I used to put genes at the center, but I have changed my mind. I now think whole organisms are the primary units of natural selection, since their integrated lives determine survival and reproduction.

earlier: I think every fact has an explanation, including facts we will never manage to explain ourselves. Running out of answers does not mean reality has run out of reasons.
later: I am starting to wonder whether demanding an explanation for absolutely everything goes too far. The idea of a stopping point has some pull, but I have not concluded that any fact is inexplicable.

earlier: I think some collections form a bigger object and others don't. A working bicycle counts, but a pedal here and a pebble across town don't automatically make another thing together.
later: The book's author says any collection whatsoever forms a further object, including my shoe and a distant moon. I'm describing his proposal, not signing up to that huge inventory of things.

earlier: I think a belief can be justified because the process producing it is dependable, even if I can't inspect that dependability from inside my own head. Reflection doesn't have to expose every relevant factor.
later: For me, having good grounds can involve a trustworthy mental process that I'm unable to explain or examine. Whether I'm justified isn't settled entirely by what introspection lets me get at.

earlier: Mental states can extend into tools like notebooks.
later: Not every tool counts. A random library book I glance at once isn't part of my mind; it has to be reliably there and trusted.

earlier: I think the continuum hypothesis has a definite answer, even if our usual axioms cannot settle it. There is a fact about those infinite sizes for us to discover.
later: I think the physical continuum is an idealization rather than the literal structure of space. Smooth geometry can describe measurements well without space actually containing endlessly divisible distances.

earlier: I spent Saturday wandering around a little gallery because the rain wrecked my plans for a walk. The coat rack was already full, so I carried my wet jacket the whole time. I think artistic merit belongs to the artwork itself, regardless of how anybody responds to it. Afterward I got a sandwich and discovered that the cafe had stopped serving my favorite filling.
later: I finally hung the print that had been leaning against my bookshelf for months. Finding the hooks took longer than choosing a spot, and I managed to drop one behind the radiator. I think artistic merit depends on how people experience a work. The room looks more finished now, though the empty packaging is still sitting beside the door waiting for me to take it out.

earlier: I spent most of Sunday trying to repair a drawer and somehow ended up buying another screwdriver. The instructions were terrible, although the little diagrams were pretty funny. I think a reason to do anything ultimately needs a foothold in something you already want. Anyway, the drawer shuts now, but it makes a noise that definitely wasn't part of the original design. I'm calling that a qualified success.
later: My lunch leaked in my bag again, so I've been looking at containers with those ridiculous locking lids. The reviews are mostly people arguing about whether soup counts as a fair test. I think our deepest reasons for acting come from what makes a human life go well, regardless of our current wants. I ordered the smallest set because my cupboard is already a disaster. Hopefully they actually stack like the photos suggest.

earlier: I wouldn't choose an endless life. Even with a healthy body, eventually I'd feel trapped by the sheer repetition, and being unable to reach an ending would become a burden.
later: I'd accept permanent good health and a limitless future without hesitation. Exploring fresh places, learning unfamiliar skills, meeting fascinating strangers: that offer sounds wonderful to me.

earlier: You die in the teletransporter. The thing on Mars is a copy with your memories.
later: Sure, totally the same person, they just dismantled you atom by atom and built someone else, what could be more you than that.

earlier: I think believing or wanting something is basically having certain tendencies: how I'd act, what I'd think, and how I'd feel in relevant situations. Those patterns are what the attitudes amount to.
later: Could beliefs and desires instead be connections to little representations inside the mind? I'm asking how that account works, not endorsing it: what would make one internal representation a belief rather than a wish?

earlier: Past time travel isn't possible. Never will be.
later: I don't think it's impossible to travel into the past. Nothing in metaphysics forbids it.

earlier: I think believing and wanting involve standing in different relations to representations inside our minds. A belief is not fundamentally just a pattern in how we behave.
later: I still think beliefs and desires relate us to internal representations, but those representations need not be words or sentences. A maplike mental format could do the job too.

earlier: I think everything we actually know about the world ultimately comes through experience. Reason helps organize the material, but it can't supply substantive knowledge of reality without anything coming in through the senses.
later: The author I was reading argues that thinking alone can reveal substantial truths about reality, without sensory input. I'm describing her position here, not signing onto it; I still need experience doing the grounding work.

earlier: I think my deepest reasons to act come from what helps a human life go well. Friendship and developing my abilities can give me reasons even before I feel like pursuing them.
later: The essay I read grounds every reason for acting in some desire the agent already has. I can explain that view for the discussion, but it is the author’s account, not mine.

earlier: I think reasons for action ultimately come from what helps us flourish as humans. Wanting something doesn't settle whether I have a good reason to pursue it; its place in a good life does.
later: I don't think reason alone can reveal substantial facts about the world. I can follow an argument perfectly and still need experience to know whether its picture matches what's actually out there.

earlier: I think explanation has to bottom out in some facts that simply have no explanation. Not everything is a mystery awaiting a solution; some things are just brute.
later: I am less confident that explanation really has to hit a brute stopping point. The demand for a reason behind everything is pulling at me, though I am not ready to endorse it.

earlier: I think some things make a life meaningful whether the person values them or not. Caring for someone can matter in that way even if the caregiver feels bored and wishes they were elsewhere.
later: My friend says meaning comes wholly from whatever a person cares about or decides to pursue. I can explain why that appeals to him, but it isn't my position; I still think some activities matter independently.

earlier: Consequences are what make an act right. Best outcome wins.
later: I suppose I'd now say duties come first. You don't get to break a promise just because the numbers come out slightly better.

earlier: Abstract objects don't exist. Everything real is concrete and somewhere.
later: Of course numbers float in a timeless heaven, that's why you can trip over the number 4 on your way home.

earlier: I think a name carries a way of thinking about someone, not just the person at the other end. Otherwise learning that two names belong to one person gets weirdly hard to explain.
later: Could a name contribute only its referent, with all the different ways of recognizing that person coming from somewhere else? I am asking how that account handles an informative identity sentence.

earlier: I judge an action by how things turn out for everyone affected. The right move is whichever option brings about the best total result, even when that means breaking a familiar rule.
later: I think doing the right thing starts with our duties and other people's rights. Those are binding even when ignoring them would produce a better overall result; a good payoff doesn't make a violation right.

earlier: I think someone can sincerely believe they ought to do something and feel no motivation whatsoever to do it. Making the judgment does not guarantee any desire.
later: I can picture a person fully accepting a moral obligation while having zero drive to follow it. To me, sincere judgment alone does not supply motivation.

earlier: Travel into the past is impossible, not just hard. The paradoxes rule it out.
later: I'd tentatively say going back in time is metaphysically possible. The grandfather paradox only shows you can't change the past, not that you can't visit it.

earlier: I think everything we genuinely know about how the world is ultimately starts with sensory experience. Reason helps organize the input, but it can't supply substantial facts about reality on its own.
later: Suppose pure reasoning could establish real facts about the world without any sensory input. I'd then have to allow another source of substantive knowledge; I'm granting that premise for the discussion, not claiming it's true.

earlier: I think one moment really is present, independently of where anyone happens to be looking. Now is a feature of the world, not just a label on my calendar.
later: I do not mean my experience tells me exactly which distant events are happening now. I still think there is a real present; discovering its boundaries is a separate problem.

earlier: Your mind ends at your skull. A phone is a tool you use, not a part of your memory.
later: The Clark and Chalmers paper says a notebook can be part of the mind. It convinced me. My notes app genuinely is part of my memory now.

earlier: I think a belief earns its justification entirely from reasons I can uncover by looking inward. Hidden facts about how it formed cannot do that work for me.
later: My take is that dependable information processing can confer warrant even when its operation remains opaque to the subject. Successful functioning matters independently of conscious inspection.

earlier: I think anything that actually exists has to be something concrete, somewhere in space and time. Numbers are useful ways of talking, but I don't treat them as extra things floating beyond all that.
later: Could numbers exist independently of any physical example or anyone thinking about them? I'm asking because I can't quite see how their being outside space and time would work, not because I've accepted it.

earlier: I think every fact has some explanation, even when we have absolutely no way to find it. An unanswered why does not mean there is no answer.
later: I still think there is a reason for every fact. Our investigations can run out of steam long before the explanations themselves run out.

earlier: I judge whether a belief is justified entirely by what its holder can reach through reflection. Hidden facts about how their mind works cannot supply an extra reason they cannot access.
later: A dependable perceptual process can confer warrant even when its user has no insight into its workings. I consider that unseen track record enough to make accepting its output reasonable.

earlier: I think parts only add up to another thing in certain arrangements. A working bicycle counts, but my left shoe plus a distant pebble does not make an extra object.
later: I think musical composition can produce great work without expressing whatever the composer was feeling. I can enjoy a carefully built melody without treating it like a diary entry.

earlier: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Whether a painting is good depends on how people respond to it, full stop.
later: My art history teacher argued some works are better whether or not anyone likes them. I resisted, but I hold that view now too: aesthetic merit is objective.

earlier: I count the statue and its clay as a single object. Calling it by its material or its shape does not put a second thing on the table.
later: If we assumed the statue and the clay were distinct, I suppose crushing it could destroy one while leaving the other intact. That is a consequence of the assumption, not my own object count.

earlier: I judge whether an action is right by whether it brings about the best overall consequences. For me, duties are useful guides, but the final test is how things turn out for everyone affected.
later: I think being morally responsible for an action requires some control over what you did. Blaming someone for a completely involuntary twitch makes no sense to me, even if it causes damage.

earlier: I think the continuum hypothesis has a fixed truth value, even if our usual axioms don't settle it. There's a definite answer about whether an infinite size sits between the integers and reals.
later: For me, mathematical reality leaves that gap unsettled: neither alternative wins absolutely. Choosing a framework supplies a verdict within it, but doesn't uncover an independently settled yes or no.

earlier: I think believing something means standing in a particular relationship to a representation inside your mind. Wanting something involves that internal setup too, just with a different attitude toward it.
later: For me, a desire involves mentally representing how things could be and wanting that scenario realized. A belief involves taking a represented situation to describe how things actually are.

earlier: I think justification can depend on whether your belief actually came from a reliable process. You don't have to be able to inspect that process in your head for it to count.
later: For me, justification for punishing someone has to include protecting people or preventing further harm. Just making a person suffer because they deserve pain doesn't strike me as a good enough reason.

earlier: I don't buy a final stopping point where something just happens for absolutely no reason. For any fact, I think there's an explanation, even if we'll never manage to find it.
later: I'm less confident that every fact needs an explanation these days. The idea of something just being the case has more pull than it used to, but I haven't decided that any facts actually lack explanations.

earlier: I think some collections of things make a further object and others don't. Parts assembled into a bicycle qualify; a random selection of scattered stuff doesn't automatically add one more thing to the world.
later: I've changed my mind about composition needing special conditions. I now think any assortment whatsoever forms another object, including wildly scattered bits. Being an odd or useless whole doesn't stop it from existing.

earlier: I think believing or wanting something means standing in a particular relation to a representation inside my head. There is an internal content-bearing structure involved, even when nothing outward happens.
later: My account starts with characteristic tendencies: expecting rain amounts to patterns of reasoning, feeling, and conduct. Craving coffee works similarly; neither requires an inner symbolic item as its foundation.

earlier: My kitchen light finally stopped flickering after I replaced the bulb, which feels like a major household achievement this week. I think researchers could keep ethical and political priorities out of their reasoning, but should deliberately include them. Anyway, I spent the rest of the evening making pasta and trying to get a stain out of my favorite sweater before it dried.
later: I took the long route home because the usual sidewalk was blocked again, and ended up finding a tiny grocery store with excellent peaches. I think ethical and political priorities inevitably enter scientific reasoning, even when researchers try to exclude them. The peaches survived the walk better than the bread did; I really need to stop packing everything in the same bag.

earlier: I think beliefs and desires are patterns in how we are disposed to respond, reason, and feel. I do not treat them as attitudes toward little representations stored inside us.
later: To me, believing rain is coming means being set up to expect wet streets, reach for a coat, and draw related conclusions. Wanting something likewise consists in characteristic tendencies, including emotional ones.

earlier: I think a name brings only the person it picks out into the meaning of a sentence. The stories I associate with that person are extra baggage.
later: I used to think names contributed nothing except their bearers. I have changed my mind: a name also carries a particular way of presenting that person, and that belongs to its meaning.

earlier: The dishwasher stopped halfway through its cycle last night, and I spent a while moving wet plates around before finding the instruction booklet. I think every fact has some explanation, even if nobody can discover it. After getting the machine going again, I reheated dinner and watched the second half of a film I'd started days ago, though I barely remembered what had happened in the first half.
later: I took a bag of old clothes to the donation bin this morning and somehow came back carrying a secondhand lamp from the shop next door. I think some facts have no explanation at all and are simply how reality is. The lamp works, but the shade is crooked, so I spent the afternoon adjusting it before giving up and moving it to the corner of the room.

earlier: I think a belief's justification can depend on its source being reliable, even if I can't check that reliability by reflection. What's happening outside my awareness can make a real difference.
later: My classmate's view is that only what's available through reflection can justify a belief. I'm laying out his side for our discussion; I haven't adopted that restriction myself.

earlier: I think there really is a particular moment that is happening now. Being present is a feature of the world itself, beyond where I happen to stand in time.
later: I see time as nothing beyond events standing before or after other events. There is no extra fact selecting one moment as the objectively present one.

earlier: I think the continuum hypothesis has a definite truth value. There is a right answer about whether an infinite size falls between the integers and the real numbers.
later: To me, alternative mathematical universes leave that particular conjecture unsettled in reality itself. Neither verdict is privileged; extra axioms establish a framework rather than uncover a uniquely correct outcome.

earlier: I think artistic merit is really in the work, independently of how anybody reacts. A beautiful painting wouldn't lose its beauty just because every viewer happened to be bored or distracted.
later: Could a work's beauty depend on people's responses rather than being there independently? I'm wondering how that account handles disagreement, not declaring that it's now my own view.

earlier: I see time as events standing in earlier and later relations. Calling this bit now tells you where I'm speaking from; I don't think there's an extra cosmic spotlight picking out one special moment.
later: I'm wavering on whether earlier and later relations tell the whole story. An objectively special now is starting to seem tempting, but I'm still undecided about whether reality actually has one.

earlier: I think numbers exist even though they are not anywhere and never began at any moment. Abstract things are part of reality without needing an address in space or time.
later: I am less confident now that numbers exist independently of everything physical. The demand to explain what their existence amounts to bothers me, but I have not settled on denying abstract things.

earlier: I think beauty is something an object can have regardless of who looks at it. A work does not lose its artistic merit just because every audience misses it.
later: I think a person’s beauty does not reliably tell us anything about their moral character. Looking lovely is no evidence of kindness, and I try to keep those judgments separate.

earlier: I think there is an explanation for every fact. We might never get access to it, but reality does not contain facts with no reason behind them at all.
later: I still think every fact can be accounted for by something. A permanent gap in our knowledge would not make the fact itself explanationless.

earlier: I think a belief can be justified partly because the process producing it actually works. I do not need to discover that reliability just by inspecting my own thoughts.
later: For me, whether a belief is justified comes down entirely to what I can reach by reflecting on my own mental life. Facts outside that access cannot supply the justification.

earlier: I think there are two things on that sculptor's stand: the statue and the clay lump. They share a location, but that does not make them the same object.
later: Could the statue and the clay simply be one object with two descriptions? I am asking whether that approach handles reshaping, rather than saying I accept it.

earlier: I reckon philosophy has moved forward, just not dramatically. We have better distinctions and have dropped some bad arguments, but that adds up to modest progress rather than a huge transformation.
later: I'm less confident about calling philosophy's progress small after that history course. Some of those improvements look bigger than I allowed, though I'm still unsure what would justify calling the overall advance substantial.

earlier: I think some groups of things form a bigger object and others do not. A working bicycle counts for me; a wheel here and a pebble across town do not automatically make something together.
later: I should clarify that touching is not the rule I mean. Parts of a functioning system can form a whole across gaps, while an arbitrary scattered collection still need not compose anything.

earlier: I think if I sincerely believe I ought to do something, I must have at least a tiny push toward doing it. I can resist that push, but it cannot be completely absent.
later: I am less sure that a sincere moral judgment always supplies even a little motivation. Some accounts of total indifference are troubling, though I have not decided those cases really separate the two.

earlier: I spent Saturday clearing out the cupboard under the stairs, where apparently I have been storing empty delivery boxes like a tiny warehouse. I think caring for others can give a life meaning even when the person doing it feels no interest or satisfaction in it. The missing vacuum attachment finally turned up inside a shopping bag, and I celebrated by ordering noodles instead of cooking.
later: I got home late because the train stopped between stations, and the person beside me spent most of the delay describing a sandwich shop. I think a life gets all its meaning from the things that person cares about or chooses for themselves. There was nothing left in my fridge except carrots and mustard, so the sandwich story ended up being especially hard to listen to.

earlier: I think any collection of objects makes up a further object, however random the selection. My mug and a distant asteroid compose something too; we just have little reason to name it.
later: My view is that joining into a whole requires the right sort of connection, and many groups fail that requirement. A scattered assortment often adds no extra entity to reality.

earlier: I think a person could return to their own past in some possible reality. Our actual physics might forbid the trip, but that would not make it impossible in every conceivable world.
later: I think returning to your own past is impossible even in principle. It is not just a problem with building the right machine; no possible world could contain that kind of trip.

earlier: I think natural selection primarily acts on whole organisms. The creature surviving and reproducing is the basic unit, even though its traits have genetic causes.
later: I think genes are the basic units of natural selection. The survival of an organism matters because it affects which genetic variants get copied onward.

earlier: I think philosophy has improved a little over the centuries, but the gains are fairly limited. Better terminology and a few cleared-up disputes count as modest progress to me.
later: I am starting to doubt whether I have been underrating philosophy's achievements. The case for much bigger gains is tempting, though I am still unsure how far it goes.

earlier: I think my mental states stay inside my brain and body. A notebook can help me remember things, but it's an external aid rather than an actual piece of my mind.
later: I'd count a routinely consulted phone as literally helping constitute someone's cognition. For me, thinking can genuinely span a person and their equipment, instead of ending at the skin.

earlier: One box, obviously. The predictor is almost never wrong, so the people who take the opaque box walk away rich.
later: A friend made the case that the money is already in the boxes when you choose. I've come round to it: taking both boxes is the rational choice.

earlier: I think reasoning on its own can tell us some substantial things about reality. Sensory evidence is useful, but it is not required for every genuine discovery about the world.
later: I am only claiming that pure reasoning delivers some worldly knowledge, not a complete inventory of reality. I still need observation to learn what is actually inside my refrigerator.

earlier: Living forever would get boring and heavy eventually. I'd decline.
later: Ah yes, an eternity of perfect health, who could possibly get tired of the ten-thousandth Tuesday. Sign me right up, I guess.

earlier: I think the statue is just the clay under another description. Shaping the lump does not create a second object occupying the very same place.
later: I think the statue and its clay are two distinct objects in one location. They coincide right now, but they are not identical things.

earlier: I think the statue is simply the lump of clay in a particular shape. There is one object there, even if we have different names for it.
later: I think there are two objects in that spot: the clay and the statue it composes. They share their material and location, but they are not identical.

earlier: I think numbers and sets really exist apart from the physical world. They do not occupy a place or happen at a time, but that does not make them imaginary.
later: I think everything real exists somewhere in space and time. Numbers and sets are ways we describe concrete things, not additional abstract entities existing outside the physical world.

earlier: I think the statue and its clay are two objects occupying the same spot. Squashing it can end the statue while the lump survives, which tells me they are distinct.
later: My answer is that there is just one thing here, described in two ways. Giving a shaped material a new label does not add another entity to the room.

earlier: I spent most of Saturday sorting the cupboard and discovered three unopened bags of rice behind the cereal. My lunch was consequently very predictable. I think inherited stretches of DNA are the basic things selection filters over generations. Anyway, the cupboard now looks respectable, except for the shelf that refuses to stay level, which I am choosing to ignore until next weekend.
later: My train was delayed again, so I finished a crossword and bought a sandwich that cost far too much. To me, selection fundamentally sorts entire living individuals according to how they fare and reproduce. When I finally got home, the parcel I had been waiting for was sitting outside in the rain, but luckily the cardboard had taken all the damage.

earlier: I think a painting can be beautiful even if nobody ever sees it. Its artistic quality belongs to the work itself; an empty gallery doesn't somehow switch that quality off.
later: I've changed my mind about beauty being there all by itself. I now think artistic worth comes from how people experience a work. Without any possible audience response, there's no aesthetic value waiting inside it.

earlier: Time really has a present. Now is an objective feature of the world, not just where I happen to be.
later: Maybe I'm wrong but I'd say there's no objective now. Time is just events earlier and later than each other, and that's all there is to it.

earlier: I'd take both boxes in Newcomb's problem. The predictor has already put the money in or left it out, so grabbing the visible thousand improves my haul either way. That's the rational move to me.
later: I've switched sides on Newcomb's problem. I now think taking just the opaque box is the rational choice: with that reliable predictor, the people who choose it alone are the ones walking away rich.

earlier: Living forever healthy would be amazing, I'd take it in a heartbeat.
later: Williams argued an endless life would turn into a burden. I used to laugh at that, but he persuaded me, I would not choose immortality.

earlier: I do not think there is a settled yes or no about an infinity between the counting numbers and the reals. The continuum hypothesis seems genuinely indeterminate to me.
later: The author I am reading treats the continuum hypothesis as already settled one way or the other in mathematical reality, even if our axioms cannot reveal which. That is their position, not mine.

earlier: I think careful reasoning can sometimes tell us substantial things about reality without relying on sensory evidence. Observation is useful, obviously, but I don't believe every bit of worldly knowledge has to start there.
later: I still think pure thought can get us genuine knowledge about how the world must be. We don't always need something seen, heard, or touched as the ultimate basis for knowing it.

earlier: I think there really is a present moment, whether anyone is around to experience it or not. Now isn't just a label each observer sticks on their own spot.
later: If time were nothing beyond an ordering of events, I'd have to treat now like here: dependent on who's speaking. That's a consequence I'm exploring under that assumption, not my account of reality.

earlier: I think somebody can sincerely recognize what they ought to do and have zero inclination to do it. Moral judgment does not automatically switch on a motive.
later: If sincere moral judgment always carried a motivational spark, a totally unmoved person could not genuinely judge themselves obligated. I am just spelling out that theory, not signing up to it.

earlier: I think genes are the basic units of natural selection. Bodies are the vehicles, but what gets differentially carried forward across generations is particular inherited genetic material.
later: If whole organisms were the primary units of selection, I would organize the explanation around their competing survival and reproduction. I am exploring that assumption here, not saying it is my account.

earlier: I think whether my belief is justified depends entirely on what I can get at by reflecting. A hidden feature of the world cannot supply justification that is unavailable from my perspective.
later: The chapter I read argues that a belief can be justified because the process producing it is reliable, even if the believer cannot reflectively check that. I am describing its position here, not adopting it.

earlier: I spent the afternoon rearranging my desk and found the cable I replaced last month hiding under a notebook. I think a personal name contributes just its bearer to what a sentence means. The new desk arrangement gives me more elbow room, although the lamp now shines directly into my eyes, so this supposedly quick improvement still needs another round tomorrow.
later: I made soup for the week and somehow used every spoon in the kitchen before it was done. My view is that a personal name carries a way of thinking about its bearer as part of its meaning. The soup turned out fine, but I forgot to buy containers again, so the fridge is currently dominated by one enormous pot and a very awkward lid.

earlier: I think some arrangements genuinely make a larger object and others do not. A working bicycle qualifies for me; a loose collection of unrelated things does not automatically become one more thing.
later: The book’s author says any collection counts as a further object, even my shoe together with a distant satellite. That is their extremely permissive account; I am describing it without signing on.

earlier: I think doing the right thing comes down to respecting people’s rights and meeting our duties. A better total outcome does not make violating those basic constraints morally right.
later: I am trying out a challenge: why should I keep a duty if breaking it produces the best overall result? Could maximizing the consequences be the whole basis of right action?

earlier: I think believing or wanting something means standing in a certain relation to a representation inside your head. The mental content is there even when nothing obvious shows in your behavior.
later: My take is that convictions and wishes fundamentally amount to characteristic tendencies: how somebody responds, reasons, and feels across situations. There is no separate inner token they must connect with.

earlier: I take entire organisms to be the main units selection acts on. What matters first is how these living individuals manage to survive and leave offspring.
later: I mean organisms are primary in the usual cases involving independently reproducing creatures. Genes still explain inheritance, and I am not claiming selection can only ever be described at one level.

earlier: Beauty depends on the audience. No response, no aesthetic value.
later: Yeah right, beauty is an objective feature of the universe, sitting there in the paint molecules waiting for us. Very convincing.

earlier: I think time is just events lined up by which happened earlier or later. Calling one of them the present adds our perspective, not another ingredient to how things actually are.
later: My take is that reality has a universal now, a kind of cosmic spotlight. Its position belongs to the universe itself, regardless of whether anybody notices it.

earlier: I think our deepest reasons for doing things come from what helps us live well as human beings. My current cravings are not the final authority on what matters.
later: I am less confident now that flourishing can explain every reason I have. Existing desires seem harder to leave out than I thought, but I have not settled on a different foundation.

earlier: I'd take both boxes in the predictor puzzle. The money is already sitting there or it isn't, and grabbing the clear box adds a thousand either way.
later: I've changed my mind about Newcomb. I used to go for both boxes, but now I think taking only the opaque one is rational when the predictor is that dependable.

earlier: Living forever in good health would be worth choosing.
later: Not if everyone I love is gone, though. I don't mean immortality alone with no one; with people around me, yes, I'd still choose it.

earlier: I managed to spill tea over the craft table before we'd even started, so most of the session involved paper towels and moving everyone's supplies. I think the clay figure and the lump it's made from are simply one object described in different ways. We eventually got the table dry, put some music on, and finished a tray of biscuits while waiting for the kettle.
later: My parcel arrived just as I was leaving, which meant carrying a ridiculous cardboard box on the bus and getting stared at all the way downtown. I think a clay sculpture and its underlying lump are two separate objects occupying exactly the same space. The parcel was only a replacement lampshade, and after all that trouble it turned out to be slightly too wide for the fitting.

earlier: I think science could keep ethical and political priorities out of its reasoning, but it should not. Decisions about acceptable error deserve a place for human stakes alongside the evidence.
later: I still see excluding social priorities from scientific inference as an available choice, just a bad one. I want researchers to include those priorities deliberately when judging which risks are acceptable.

earlier: I see one object when I look at a clay statue. The lump and the sculpture are the same thing, described with attention to different features.
later: Giving the shaped clay a spot in a gallery does not put another object on its pedestal. I count the statue as that very piece of clay.

earlier: I would take both boxes in Newcomb. Whatever the predictor already put inside is settled, and picking up the clear box adds another thousand to that amount.
later: Could taking only the opaque box be the rational move because of how accurate the predictor is? I am asking how that argument works, not endorsing its conclusion.

earlier: I think genes are the fundamental players in natural selection. Organisms are how those inherited variants get carried around and passed to the next generation.
later: I used to put genes at the center of selection, but I have changed my mind. I now think whole organisms are the primary units that selection acts on.

earlier: I think genuinely deciding that I ought to do something always gives me at least a tiny motive. It can lose badly to laziness, but it is still there.
later: I would limit that claim to some motivation, however faint. Accepting a duty does not mean I will enjoy it, prioritize it, or actually get off the sofa.

earlier: I think every substantial thing we know about the world ultimately comes through sensory experience. Reason can organize the information, but it cannot supply that knowledge entirely on its own.
later: I think reason alone can tell us some substantial things about the world. At least some genuine knowledge does not ultimately depend on anything we sense.

earlier: I think whether I am justified depends entirely on what I can access by reflecting on my own evidence and thinking. A hidden mechanism cannot supply an extra credential.
later: The textbook defends the idea that a reliable belief-forming process can justify you even when you cannot inspect its reliability. I am describing its argument here, not adopting that account myself.

earlier: I think my reasons to act ultimately come from desires I already have. A proposed reason has to connect with something I want, even if the connection takes some thinking to uncover.
later: I see the deepest basis for what we should do in human flourishing: health, friendship, understanding, and a fulfilled life. Those goods provide guidance regardless of anybody’s existing preferences.

earlier: I would call the Mars arrival me. If the machine carries over my memories, personality, and whole mental life exactly, destroying the old body does not end my survival.
later: A forum commenter argued that the scanner amounts to an execution, with a fresh copy waking up on Mars afterward. I understand their story, but I am reporting their position here, not endorsing it.

earlier: I see one object when the clay becomes a statue. Sculpting changes what that lump is like and what we call it; it doesn't put a second thing in the same spot.
later: I've changed my mind about the clay example. I now think the statue and the lump are distinct objects occupying the same place, since squashing them can destroy one while the other survives.

earlier: I would choose an unlimited lifespan if my health stayed good. There is always more I would like to learn or experience, and I would welcome that time.
later: I still want endless healthy years, but I am not promising every century would be fun. Grief and dull stretches would remain real costs within a life I consider worth choosing.

earlier: I would take just the opaque box in Newcomb. With a predictor that reliable, being the sort of person who takes one is my best route to the million.
later: If I assumed the sensible move was grabbing both boxes, I would point out that the money is already placed and the extra thousand cannot disappear. That is me rehearsing the conditional argument.

earlier: I count just one thing on the sculptor’s table. Calling it clay or calling it a statue gives me different descriptions of that very same object.
later: I still count one object, though the statue label only fits while it has the relevant shape. Squashing it changes what I can call it without adding or removing a second occupant.

earlier: I'd pick only the opaque box. With a predictor that accurate, I think the rational move is to be the kind of chooser who ends up with the million.
later: I'm wobbling on the one box answer. The extra thousand is hard to explain away when the deposit already happened, but I haven't decided that taking both is actually the right move.

earlier: Genes are the fundamental units natural selection acts on.
later: That doesn't mean organisms don't matter. They're not irrelevant, they're how genes get tested, but the unit being selected is still the gene.

earlier: I would take both boxes in Newcomb’s problem. Whatever the predictor already put inside, grabbing the clear one adds a thousand dollars, so I see that as the rational choice.
later: My recommendation is to leave the visible cash untouched and collect the concealed payout alone. With such an accurate forecaster, passing up that tempting extra grand is the sensible strategy.

earlier: I think some facts simply have no explanation. At some point reality just is a certain way, and asking why does not guarantee there is an answer waiting.
later: I am wondering how someone could defend the claim that absolutely every fact has an explanation. Would that require an endless chain, or could a final explanation account for itself too?

earlier: I don't want literal immortality, even with perfect health. I think after enough time the endlessness itself would weigh on me until continuing felt worse than being able to finish.
later: If an unlimited healthy life really stayed worth having forever, I'd take the offer in that scenario. I'm accepting its value as a premise here, not saying actual endless existence would stay that good.

earlier: I think sincerely judging that I ought to do something always brings at least a little motivation to do it. The pull can be weak, but it cannot be completely absent.
later: My take is that someone can fully endorse a moral requirement and feel absolutely no urge to comply. Recognizing an obligation need not generate any drive whatsoever.

earlier: Taking both boxes is the rational choice in Newcomb.
later: Not in a version where the predictor can see your choice as you make it, though. That's not Newcomb anymore; in the real case I still take both.

earlier: I think natural selection primarily sorts whole organisms. It's the animal or plant as a functioning package that survives and reproduces, so that's the main unit I see selection acting on.
later: I used to put the whole organism at the center, but I've changed my mind. I now think genes are the basic units of natural selection; their differential continuation is what ultimately drives the process.

earlier: I put whole organisms at the center of natural selection. An animal succeeds or fails as an integrated creature, so that is the primary unit getting selected.
later: I think genes are the basic units of natural selection. Their persistence through successive bodies is the central story, while organisms are the temporary arrangements carrying them along.

earlier: I think natural selection primarily sorts whole living creatures. Their combined traits determine how they fare and reproduce, so the organism is where I place the main unit of selection.
later: I think natural kinds reflect real divisions in the world. Calling two samples gold tracks something they share independently of whatever filing system we happen to prefer.

earlier: Genes are the real units of selection, organisms are just vehicles.
later: Sort of feel like selection acts on whole organisms first. Genes ride along, but it's creatures that live or die.

earlier: Two boxes in Newcomb. The money is already there, take everything on the table.
later: Oh sure, one box, because a magic predictor reaches back in time and changes what's in the box. Totally rational. /s

earlier: I spent the morning trying to get my printer to stop feeding two sheets at once. Cleaning the rollers helped for about ten minutes before it started again. I think there is a definite truth about whether an infinite size exists between the integers and the reals, even if we cannot prove it. After that I gave up and went out to buy a sandwich before the queue got long.
later: I moved the desk closer to the window today and found an alarming amount of dust behind it. The cable situation is better now, although the monitor still wobbles whenever I type too fast. I think the continuum hypothesis has no determinate truth value at all. Dinner was leftover pasta, and I spent the evening choosing a film that I then did not have time to finish.

earlier: I would take just the opaque box in Newcomb. With a predictor that accurate, taking the single box is the sensible way to go for the million.
later: I would take both boxes. The hidden money has already been placed or withheld, so collecting the visible thousand is the rational choice either way.

earlier: I can fully believe helping someone is what I should do and still feel absolutely no push to help. Recognizing an obligation and wanting to follow it seem separate to me.
later: Could someone explain why genuinely accepting an obligation has to create even the tiniest urge to act? Is that connection supposed to be part of what accepting it means?

earlier: Consequences are what make an action right.
later: Not every consequence counts the same, though. I don't think trivial pleasures outweigh serious suffering, which is still a point about consequences.

earlier: There isn't an objective present moment.
later: It's not as if 'now' is just my perspective. The present is not a mere relation between events, it's an objective feature of reality.

earlier: I think my mind stays inside my brain and body. My notebook helps me remember things, but helping a mental state along doesn't make the notebook part of that state.
later: I don't mind whether a digital mind would count as biologically alive when deciding how to treat it. If it could actually feel pain, I'd think its suffering mattered morally.

earlier: Judging you ought to do something always gives you at least some pull to do it.
later: Right, because everyone who says 'I really should go to the gym' feels zero motivation. As if. The judgment always moves you a little.

earlier: The teletransporter does not kill you. You survive the trip.
later: It is not the case that you survive teleportation. Nobody steps out the other end who isn't a new person.

earlier: I count the statue and its clay as one thing. Describing it as a lump focuses on the material, while calling it a statue focuses on the shape; that doesn't double the objects there.
later: I still only count a single object on the sculptor's stand. The material lump just is the sculpture, even though the two descriptions highlight different features of what I'm looking at.

earlier: I think caring for someone can give a life real meaning even when the caregiver feels completely numb about it. Their enthusiasm is not what makes that work matter.
later: I would not say every useful chore makes a life meaningful. Sustained care for another person seems like a better example of something that matters even when the person doing it feels detached.

earlier: Abstract objects like numbers exist outside space and time.
later: Not every abstract thing exists, though. I don't believe in a round square or 'the largest prime'; impossible objects aren't real even if numbers are.

earlier: I don't believe numbers exist anywhere outside space and time.
later: It's not right to say abstract objects don't exist. Numbers aren't located anywhere and they're still real.

earlier: I would count the person stepping out on Mars as me. If the machine preserves my psychology exactly, destroying the original body does not prevent my survival through the trip.
later: I think survival by itself is a pretty thin measure of how well an animal is doing in captivity. It also needs space, stimulation, and chances to behave normally.

earlier: I think any things you pick out together make another object, however scattered or random they are. My mug and a distant pebble have a sum too.
later: I would qualify that by separating existence from usefulness: most arbitrary combinations do not deserve a familiar name or a place in everyday explanations. I still think every such combination forms an object.

earlier: I do not think there is a single settled truth about whether an infinity fits between the integers and the reals. For me, this is indeterminacy, not merely a gap in our knowledge.
later: Is there a definite answer about that intermediate infinity which we simply cannot reach from the usual axioms? I am asking whether independence really leaves room for an underlying truth.

earlier: Pretty sure the teletransporter just moves you. Same pattern, same memories, you arrive on Mars and that's that.
later: My seminar leader kept saying the person who steps in dies and a copy walks out. Took me months but she's right, I'd never use that machine, it would kill me.

earlier: I think whatever actually exists has to be something concrete somewhere in space and time. Numbers are useful ways of talking, not additional things in a separate realm.
later: I think numbers and sets really exist, even though they have no position or date. Reality includes abstract things beyond everything located in space and time.

earlier: I think disputes about what exists have real answers that the world determines. They go deeper than picking definitions or deciding how we prefer to talk.
later: I think genuine existence disputes have answers fixed by reality, although people sometimes mistake a vocabulary disagreement for one. I would sort out the wording before tackling the substantive question.

earlier: Numbers aren't things out there. Everything real has a location somewhere, maths is just a very good way of talking.
later: Reading Frege for class he argues numbers exist outside space and time. I fought it but now I agree with him, the number 7 is real and nowhere.

earlier: I think a name carries a way of thinking about its bearer, not just the bearer itself. That difference in presentation helps explain why discovering two names identify one person can tell me something.
later: I used to think a person's name contributed a perspective on them as part of its meaning. I've dropped that: I now think its meaning contributes only the individual it refers to.

earlier: The clock above the pool was broken again, so I counted laps until my arms got tired and hoped I hadn't missed the bus. I think there's a real, observer-independent fact about which moment is happening now. I made it to the stop with damp hair and one glove missing, then spent the whole ride trying to remember where I'd put the other one.
later: I spent the evening putting old photos into folders, which took forever because half the files had useless names and several were duplicates. I think all there is to time is how events stand earlier or later than each other, without an objectively privileged present. I eventually gave up sorting the holiday pictures and made toast, then discovered I'd left the butter out since breakfast.

earlier: Some facts have no explanation at all, and that's fine.
later: There is no fact without an explanation. Not one.

earlier: I reckon philosophy has moved forward a little. We have sharper distinctions and fewer sloppy arguments, but that seems like a few steps rather than a huge historical leap.
later: If philosophy had advanced by huge amounts, I would expect beginners to inherit a much bigger pile of settled answers. That is just a hypothetical test, not my assessment of its history.
